players.product: Helios trapped-ion quantum computer (Quantum Charge-Coupled Device architecture)

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Nitesh Sharan: second-quarter revenue was $8 million, up 279% from the prior year, driven primarily by significant growth in the cloud business and well diversified across customer type and geography, with a roughly equal split within and outside the U.S.; cost of sales was $10.3 million including roughly $6.3 million of stock-based compensation; non-GAAP gross margin was 62%; adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $68 million versus a loss of $43.5 million a year earlier; total GAAP net loss was $596.5 million ($65.4 million attributable to Quantinuum Inc.) and non-GAAP net loss $73 million ($0.28 loss per share); stock-based compensation totalled $447.5 million, a majority one-time catch-up from the IPO trigger on employee grants. First call as a public company after the June IPO.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 revenue $8 million (+279% YoY); non-GAAP gross margin 62%; adjusted EBITDA loss $68 million

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Nitesh Sharan: bookings during the second quarter were $4.3 million; including Oracle and other deals that closed after quarter end, year-to-date bookings stand at approximately $81 million, and given the visibility in its advanced pipeline Quantinuum expects at least $120 million of bookings for full-year 2026; remaining performance obligations as of Q2 were roughly $74 million (to be filed in the 10-Q); the pipeline, 'currently in the billions of dollars', spans upgrades from prior system sales, active Helios opportunities and Sol and Apollo engagements targeted to close over the next several years.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 bookings $4.3 million; YTD bookings approximately $81 million; FY2026 bookings at least $120 million; RPO roughly $74 million

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Nitesh Sharan: first formal guidance as a public company - 2026 revenue expected in the range of $28 million-$32 million, 'an increase relative to where we thought we would be at this point in the year'; from current bookings and backlog Quantinuum 'can already see revenue growth of more than 100% next year' from the 2026 outlook (based on current estimates and assumptions on contract timing and revenue recognition); quarterly results may be volatile. Long term, gross margin should be north of 50% on a sustained basis; in the Apollo timeframe Quantinuum expects to realize a significant share of what is expected to be a $10+ billion end-user value quantum market, putting its own revenue in the billions of dollars and generating positive free cash flow in 2030 and beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 revenue $28 million-$32 million; revenue growth of more than 100% next year; long-term gross margin north of 50%

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Raj Hazra: the hardware roadmap is on plan - Sol is on track for release in 2027 (second half of 2027), designed to provide 192 physical qubits and 100 logical qubits with a logical error rate of 10 to the power minus five (five nines logical fidelity), the first commercial system on the roadmap to use the two-dimensional QCCD trap chip; Sol is 'now in production build'. Apollo, which Quantinuum calls the first fully fault-tolerant quantum system, is scheduled for launch in 2029 - designs complete, now prototyping (novel laser delivery, no integrated optics); the generation after, Lumos, will tile multiple Apollo-type chips with advanced packaging, and Quantinuum has demonstrated in the lab moving qubits from one tile to another. CFO Nitesh Sharan: Quantinuum is concurrently investing in four generations of systems (Helios, Sol, Apollo, Lumos).
quarterly_data.figure: Sol (2027): 192 physical qubits, 100 logical qubits; Apollo 2029

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Raj Hazra: in the second quarter a new family of quantum error-correction codes allowed Quantinuum to demonstrate near five-nines logical fidelities on Helios (near 10 to the power -5, with fewer logical qubits), after reaching four nines on Helios last year; an exhaustive technical paper is to be published in the next two to three weeks; Quantinuum has 'already demonstrated how to do fault-tolerant T gates today' and expects Apollo to support a universal gate set. Helios, introduced in November 2025, takes about 60 kilowatts without the HVAC system versus 20 to 35 MW for a supercomputer of similar computational pedigree, and moved to a closed-loop cryogenic system that reuses helium for higher uptime and lower total cost of ownership.
quarterly_data.figure: near five-nines logical fidelity on Helios; Helios about 60 kilowatts (vs 20 to 35 MW supercomputer)

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Raj Hazra: during the second quarter Quantinuum strengthened its supply chain and scaled its manufacturing ecosystem, with strategic partnerships with GlobalFoundries (critical integrated photonics and cryogenic electronics capabilities) and Monarch Quantum (high-reliability photonic components) to build or extend its supply chain to onshore suppliers. It also signed a new joint development agreement with an unnamed 'leading global electronics manufacturer' to incorporate scaled data-center systems manufacturing, raise throughput and hit cost targets ('more on this to come soon'). CEO: an executive order calls for a fault-tolerant quantum computer to be purchased by the U.S. government and made available for science in 2028.

CFO Nitesh Sharan: research and development expenses were $367 million including $294.9 million of IPO-related stock-based compensation (versus $39.7 million a year ago); sales and marketing $29.3 million (versus $3.4 million) including roughly $17.2 million of stock-based compensation; G&A $151.9 million (versus $6.1 million) including $129 million of stock-based compensation. Quantinuum ended the quarter with approximately $2.1 billion of cash and equivalents; cash used in operating activities was $66.2 million and capital expenditures $16.6 million; excluding one-time IPO costs it expects incremental investment relative to first-half spend levels, including with supply chain partners.
quarterly_data.figure: R&D $367 million; capex $16.6 million; cash approximately $2.1 billion

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Raj Hazra: more than 180 organizations now build applications on Quantinuum Nexus, its cloud hybrid development platform (about 150 at the IPO two months earlier), with depth of use rising and driving increased cloud usage; access to the Guppy programming language was expanded through the web-based Guppy Playpond; Qedma integrated its quantum error suppression and mitigation software into Quantinuum's platform through the startup partner program. CEO: together with NVIDIA and a Fortune 100 pharma company Quantinuum demonstrated AI-driven quantum simulation for molecular property characterization ('GenQ AI'), and advanced customer programs in aerospace, energy exploration and semiconductors.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 180 organizations on Nexus (about 150 at IPO)

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Raj Hazra: demand is broad across platform generations - on-premises demand continues to grow, including sovereign ecosystems similar to the Singapore model and regional ecosystems in the U.S., there is good demand for Helios cycles, and demand for Apollo as a follow-on to installed systems; no decision yet on building Sol systems differently (on-premises), 'but we're obviously thinking about those very actively because the demand is forcing us to do that'. CFO Nitesh Sharan: Quantinuum sees upgrades of existing previous sales and expansion of cloud usage; the mix is expected to shift from system sales toward software and services, making revenue more ratable with a better margin profile; the indirect channel (Oracle, HPE and others) is a key growth area.

connects_to.relationship: Helios quantum computer offered through OCI, installed in a U.S.-based OCI AI data center

contracts.signal: CEO Raj Hazra: in the strategic partnership announced the day of the call, Oracle is purchasing a Helios that goes on-premises into an OCI data center in the U.S., tightly integrated as an OCI service with OCI networking, compute, storage, identity management and data services and Quantinuum's software stack; it will be the first Helios in a data center on U.S. soil beyond Quantinuum's own (the other announced system is headed for Singapore); focus areas include drug discovery, material science, new energy sources and pharma; financial details not disclosed. CFO Nitesh Sharan: 'a meaningful deal' and multi-year; some initial activation via cloud captures a little revenue this year, while most revenue comes when the system is delivered, partly contemplated in the early 2027 outlook; it is included in year-to-date bookings of approximately $81 million.
contracts.date_signed: announced the day of the call
